text: Every Barça training session starts the same way. A circle of players, two defenders in the middle, and one rule: don't lose the ball.
It's called a rondo. And for nearly twenty years, nobody in the world played it better than Xavi Hernández.
Two defenders close him down. One touch. The ball is gone — and still ours.
In this video you'll learn the three habits that made Xavi almost impossible to take the ball from: the angle, the turn and the pause.
And at the end, the drill that ties them together — the same one Barça's youngest players do every day.
Xavi grew up in Terrassa, near Barcelona, and joined the club's academy when he was eleven.
He made his first-team debut in nineteen ninety-eight. For years, people said he was too small and too slow for modern football.

Then he became the heartbeat of the greatest era in Spanish football history: European champion in two thousand and eight — when he was named the player of the tournament — world champion in twenty ten, and European champion again in twenty twelve.
He played seven hundred and sixty-seven official games for Barça, a club record until Messi passed it. Small and slow, it turned out, didn't matter. What mattered was his brain.
Habit one. The angle.
Here's a midfielder standing directly behind an opponent. The centre-back can't pass to him. He's in the opponent's shadow.
Xavi was obsessed with getting out of that shadow. Two or three steps to the side — and suddenly there's a clear line between him and the ball.
It sounds small. But if you're always available, your team almost never has to play a risky pass.
He was famous for constantly moving his head, looking for space before the ball came. His whole game started there.

The most common mistake is standing still and waiting for the ball. Football is moving, so your angle is always changing. Every time the ball moves, ask yourself: can the player with the ball see me right now?
Drill: in any passing game, after every pass you make, take two steps to a new position before the ball comes back. Never stay in the spot where you passed it from.
Habit two. The turn.
Now the pressure arrives. A defender charges in from behind.
Xavi's answer was a little spin: he'd feel the defender, let him commit, and roll the ball away with the sole or the inside of his foot, turning his body between the man and the ball.
Half a second later, he's facing forward, with the defender behind him, and the pass is on.
The key word is feel. He didn't need to see the defender, because he'd already looked before receiving — and he could feel the contact.
The mistake is turning towards the pressure, straight into the defender. Always turn away from where the pressure is coming from.

Drill: ask a friend to stand behind you and lean on you gently while you receive. Practise rolling the ball away from their side, again and again, with both feet. Then ask them to push a little harder.
Habit three. The pause.
Here's a defender standing between two of Xavi's teammates. If Xavi passes too early, the defender just steps across and intercepts.
So Xavi waits. Just a moment, with the ball under control, until the defender leans one way.
And then he plays it the other way.
In Spain they call this la pausa — the pause. It's one of the hardest skills in football, because it means staying calm with the ball when everything in your body is telling you to get rid of it.

The mistake is confusing a pause with being slow. The pause is only useful if you've already seen both options. You're not waiting to think — you're waiting for the defender to make his decision first.
Drill: two-against-one. You and a teammate against one defender, in a small box. You're not allowed to pass until the defender has moved towards one of you. It forces you to watch him, not the ball.
And now the drill that ties it all together. The rondo.
Make a square about ten metres by ten. Four players around the outside, two defenders in the middle.
The outside players can use two touches at most. When that gets easy, one touch.
Whoever loses the ball swaps into the middle.
Count your passes, and try to beat your record every session.
Notice what it trains: the angle, because you have to move to stay available. The turn, when a defender closes you down. And the pause, because the defenders are always trying to read your pass.
So, your checklist. Get out of the shadow — always be a passing option.
Turn away from the pressure, with your body between the defender and the ball.
And when you can, pause — and let the defender choose first.
Xavi later became Barça's coach, and won the league in twenty twenty-three. But his greatest lesson was the one he taught as a player: if you never lose the ball, the other team can never hurt you.
